title: Half-life and uses of radiation
examTip: Half-life calculations: each half-life halves the activity. After n half-lives, remaining activity = initial × (1/2)ⁿ. Read this off a graph, or calculate it. The exam often gives you a decay graph. It asks you to find the half-life. See how long the activity takes to drop from one value to exactly half.
introTips: Radioactive decay is random. You cannot predict when any one nucleus will decay. But with large numbers, the overall rate is very predictable.
Half-life is the time for half the undecayed nuclei to decay. In other words, it is the time for the activity to halve.
A short half-life means the substance decays quickly. This is useful for medical tracers. A long half-life means it stays radioactive for a very long time.
Contamination means radioactive material gets onto or inside the body. Irradiation means the body is exposed to a radiation source nearby. These are different hazards.
Uses of radiation match the type of radiation to the job. Gamma is for medical imaging and sterilisation. Alpha is for smoke detectors. Beta is for thickness gauges.
intro: Every radioactive substance decays at its own rate. Some elements are so unstable that they decay in milliseconds. Others have been decaying since the Big Bang and will carry on for billions of years. Half-life is how we measure this rate. It turns out to be one of the most useful ideas in all of science. It lets archaeologists date bones that are tens of thousands of years old. It helps doctors give targeted cancer treatments. It lets engineers sterilise surgical equipment. Half-life also tells you how long radioactive waste stays dangerous. That is central to debates about nuclear power.

keyPoints.heading: What half-life means
keyPoints.content: Half-life is the time taken for the activity of a radioactive sample to halve. Put another way, it is the time for half the undecayed nuclei in a sample to decay. Radioactive decay is random. You cannot predict which nucleus will decay next, or when. But with very large numbers of atoms, the overall rate is predictable. This is why half-life is a reliable measure, even though each decay is random. Activity (measured in becquerels, Bq) is the number of decays per second. - After 1 half-life: activity = A₀/2 - After 2 half-lives: activity = A₀/4 - After 3 half-lives: activity = A₀/8 - After n half-lives: activity = A₀ × (½)ⁿ The number of undecayed nuclei halves at the same rate as the activity.
writeBullets: Half-life — the time for the activity (or number of undecayed nuclei) to halve
Activity is measured in becquerels (Bq) = number of decays per second
Radioactive decay is random. You cannot predict single decays, but the overall rate is predictable
After n half-lives: activity = initial activity × (½)ⁿ
Decay graph: a curved line that falls steeply, then flattens. It never reaches zero

keyTerms.def: The time for the activity of a radioactive sample (or number of undecayed nuclei) to halve
The number of radioactive decays per second; measured in becquerels (Bq)
The unit of radioactive activity; 1 Bq = 1 decay per second

keyPoints.memTip: Each half-life, divide the activity by 2. After 3 half-lives, divide by 8 (= 2 × 2 × 2).
keyPoints.tutor_note: Practise reading half-life from a graph. Find a point, then find half that value. Read the time difference from the x-axis.

keyPoints.heading: Reading and drawing decay graphs
keyPoints.content: A radioactive decay graph shows activity (Bq) on the y-axis and time on the x-axis. The shape is always a curved decrease that approaches but never reaches zero. This is an exponential decay curve. To find the half-life from a graph: (1) pick any starting activity value (for example, 800 Bq) (2) find half that value (400 Bq) (3) read the time at 800 Bq (t₁) and the time at 400 Bq (t₂) (4) half-life = t₂ − t₁ You can check by repeating from 400 Bq → 200 Bq. The time interval should be the same. To draw a decay graph, plot points at each half-life (0, t½, 2t½, 3t½, ...). The activity halves each time. Then join them with a smooth curve. The curve must never touch or cross the x-axis.
writeBullets: Decay graph: an exponential curve. Steep at first, flattening slowly, never reaching zero
To find half-life: pick an activity value, find half of it, and read the time difference
Half-life is constant. It takes the same time to go from 800→400 Bq as from 400→200 Bq
To draw: halve the activity at each half-life. Join with a smooth curve that never touches the x-axis
Activity in Bq on the y-axis. Time (s, min, hours or years) on the x-axis

keyTerms.def: A curve where the quantity halves in equal time intervals — the shape of all radioactive decay graphs
A graph of activity vs time showing an exponential curve — used to determine half-life

keyPoints.memTip: Pick any two points where the activity halves. The time between them is the half-life. Check it is the same anywhere on the curve.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Practise both reading half-life from graphs AND drawing decay curves. Both come up in exams.

keyPoints.heading: Uses of radioactive isotopes
keyPoints.content: Different isotopes are chosen for different jobs. The choice depends on their type of radiation and their half-life. Carbon-14 dating: half-life ~5,700 years; beta emitter. Living things take in carbon-14 (from CO₂). When they die, the C-14 decays and is not replaced. Measuring the C-14 activity left gives the age of organic remains. This works up to ~50,000 years. Medical tracers: a radioactive isotope is injected or swallowed. It travels to the target organ and is detected by a gamma camera outside the body. It must be a gamma emitter, so it gets out through the body. It must have a short half-life (days), to reduce the radiation dose. Example: technetium-99m (half-life ~6 hours). Radiotherapy (cancer treatment): a focused gamma beam kills cancer cells. Sterilisation: gamma radiation kills bacteria on surgical instruments. No chemicals are needed. Smoke detectors: americium-241 (alpha emitter, half-life ~430 years) ionises the air in the detector. When smoke blocks the ions, the alarm goes off.
writeBullets: Carbon-14 dating — beta emitter, half-life 5,700 years. Dates organic material up to ~50,000 years old
Medical tracers — gamma emitter with a short half-life (days). Injected, then detected outside the body
Technetium-99m — gamma, half-life ~6 hours. A widely used medical tracer
Sterilisation — gamma radiation kills bacteria on surgical equipment without chemicals
Smoke detectors — americium-241, alpha emitter, half-life 430 years. It ionises air; smoke breaks the current → alarm

keyTerms.def: A radioactive isotope (gamma emitter, short half-life) used to track movement through the body and detected externally
Using the known half-life of C-14 (5,700 years) to determine the age of organic remains
A widely used medical gamma-emitting tracer with a half-life of ~6 hours

keyPoints.memTip: Tracer: gamma + short half-life. Smoke detector: alpha (Am-241).
keyPoints.tutor_note: Exams often ask 'why must the tracer have a short half-life?'. Answer: to keep the patient's total radiation dose as low as possible.

keyPoints.heading: Contamination, irradiation and radiation dangers
keyPoints.content: Irradiation: being exposed to a source of radiation from outside the body. The source is not touching you or inside you. Remove the source, and the irradiation stops. Example: standing near a radioactive rock. Contamination: radioactive material gets onto or into the body. It may be on skin or clothes, or swallowed or breathed in. The material keeps irradiating you, even when you move away from other sources. It is much harder to deal with. It is very dangerous if it is an alpha emitter. Alpha is highly ionising inside the body. Why radiation is dangerous: - ionising radiation knocks electrons off atoms in body cells - this damages DNA - that can cause cancer (uncontrolled cell division) - or it can cause genetic mutations (if reproductive cells are affected) High doses can cause radiation sickness (rapid cell death). The risk grows with the dose and depends on the type of radiation. Alpha is the most ionising, so it is the most dangerous inside the body. Protection: distance, shielding (lead or concrete) and keeping exposure time short.
writeBullets: Irradiation — exposed to a radiation source from outside. Stops when the source is removed
Contamination — radioactive material on or in the body. It keeps irradiating you even when you move away
Ionising radiation damages DNA → cancer or genetic mutation
Alpha is the most dangerous in contamination. It is highly ionising near body cells
Protection: increase distance, use lead or concrete shielding, keep exposure time short

keyTerms.def: Exposure to radiation from an external source — stops when the source is removed
Radioactive material that enters or contacts the body — continues to cause exposure even when removed from the radiation area

keyPoints.memTip: Irradiation = from outside, stops with distance. Contamination = on or in the body, stays with you.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Contamination vs irradiation is a classic exam question. Give an example of each. Explain why contamination is more serious.

0.question: A radioactive sample has an initial activity of 640 Bq. After 3 half-lives, what is the activity?
0.correctFeedback: Correct! After 3 half-lives: 640 → 320 → 160 → 80 Bq. Each half-life divides by 2. So after 3: 640 ÷ 8 = 80 Bq.
0.wrongFeedback: Divide by 2 three times: 640 → 320 → 160 → 80 Bq. Or use: 640 × (½)³ = 640 × (1/8) = 80 Bq.

1.question: On a decay graph, the activity falls from 600 Bq to 300 Bq in 4 hours. How long does it take to fall from 300 Bq to 150 Bq?
1.correctFeedback: Correct! Each fall to half takes one half-life. The half-life is 4 hours, so 300 Bq to 150 Bq also takes 4 hours.
1.wrongFeedback: The half-life stays the same. Going from 600 Bq to 300 Bq is one half-life, 4 hours. So 300 Bq to 150 Bq also takes 4 hours.

2.question: Why must the radioactive tracer used in medical imaging have a short half-life?
options: To keep the patient's total radiation dose as low as possible
To make it easier to detect outside the body
So the tracer reaches all organs equally
To stop the tracer decaying before it is injected
2.correctFeedback: Correct! With a short half-life, the tracer quickly decays to a very low activity. So the patient gets a much smaller total radiation dose.
2.wrongFeedback: The half-life must be short to keep the total radiation dose low. Once the imaging is done, you want the activity to fall quickly. Then the patient is not exposed to ongoing radiation.

3.question: What is the key difference between contamination and irradiation?
options: Contamination: radioactive material is on or in the body, and keeps irradiating you as you move. Irradiation: exposure from an outside source, which stops when the source is removed
Contamination is always from gamma radiation. Irradiation is always from alpha
Contamination only affects the skin. Irradiation affects internal organs
Irradiation means the body becomes radioactive. Contamination does not
3.correctFeedback: Exactly right! Contamination: radioactive material is on or in the body, so the risk goes wherever you go. Irradiation: an outside source. Remove the source or move away, and the exposure stops.
3.wrongFeedback: The key difference is location. Contamination = radioactive material on or in the body (it stays with you). Irradiation = an outside source (it stops when the source is removed or you move away).

commonMistakes: Dividing by n instead of using (½)ⁿ. After 3 half-lives, divide by 8 (= 2³), not by 3.
Saying the activity reaches zero. It never does. The curve gets closer and closer to zero but never arrives.
Mixing up contamination and irradiation. Contamination means radioactive material is on or in the body. Irradiation is outside exposure only.
Choosing an isotope with the wrong half-life for a medical tracer. A very long half-life gives a needlessly high radiation dose. Too short, and it decays before the imaging is done.
Forgetting to explain why a medical tracer must give out gamma. It must pass through the body to reach a camera outside. Alpha or beta would be absorbed before reaching the detector.
examTips: To find half-life from a graph: pick a clear starting point and halve the activity. Read both times from the x-axis and subtract. Check your answer by repeating from the second point.
After n half-lives: remaining activity = initial × (½)ⁿ. If you are not confident with powers, build a step-by-step table.
For 'why gamma for a medical tracer' questions: (1) gamma passes through tissue. So it can be detected outside the body. (2) A short half-life means the dose falls quickly after the scan.
Contamination is harder to deal with than irradiation, because the source stays with you. Mention this when explaining why alpha contamination is so dangerous.
